nameStory: Marsh Hay Cordgrass gets its "hay" name because early colonists harvested this tough salt marsh grass to feed their livestock during winter months. The "cordgrass" part comes from its wiry, rope-like stems that feel almost like thin cord when you roll them between your fingers. It was so valuable as winter fodder that entire communities would gather in the marshes each fall for the "salt hay harvest."
description: Marsh Hay Cordgrass is a slender, wiry grass that forms thick, springy mats in coastal salt marshes. Growing 1-2 feet tall, this perennial grass has hollow stems that bend easily in the wind, creating a distinctive "cowlicked" appearance across the marsh. It's green in spring and summer, turning a warm light brown in fall and winter. The narrow leaves roll inward, making them appear almost round rather than flat like typical grass blades.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow leaves that roll inward lengthwise, appearing almost round or tube-like rather than flat - run your finger along one and you'll feel the curved, hollow shape

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms thick, bouncy mats that bend and swirl in the wind, creating a "field of cowlicks" pattern across the marsh - the weak stems can't stand straight in coastal breezes

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Deep purple flower spikes from June to October that grow along only one side of the stem, turning brown in winter - look like tiny brushes attached to the stem

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Wispy, hollow stems that feel thin and wiry between your fingers, bending easily without breaking when you gently push against them

habitat: Found in the upper zones of coastal salt marshes throughout New England, where it's occasionally covered by high tides but not constantly flooded. Look for it in brackish areas where salt and fresh water mix, often growing alongside Saltmarsh Cordgrass in slightly higher, less salty spots. It can also colonize sandy beaches and areas disturbed by storm overwash.

seasonality.spring: New green growth emerges, with the fresh shoots appearing bright green against last year's brown, matted stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and turn lush green, with deep purple flower spikes beginning to appear by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Purple flowers mature and plants begin turning from green to light brown, creating beautiful golden-brown waves across the marsh.
seasonality.winter: Completely brown and dormant, forming thick, protective mats that you can walk across - the distinctive rolled leaves and one-sided seed heads remain visible.

funFact: This grass has specialized cells that actually exclude salt from entering its roots, acting like tiny biological bouncers that keep the harmful salt out while letting fresh water in - it's like having a selective security system at the cellular level!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Saltmarsh Cordgrass, but Marsh Hay Cordgrass grows in slightly higher, less salty areas and has that distinctive "cowlicked" growth pattern from its weak stems, while Saltmarsh Cordgrass stands more upright and grows in the lowest, saltiest parts of the marsh.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently reclassified in 2014 from the genus Spartina to Sporobolus, so you might still see it listed as "Spartina patens" in older field guides and reference materials. Both names refer to the same distinctive salt marsh grass.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Saltmarsh Cordgrass which grows tall and sturdy in the lowest marsh zones, Marsh Hay Cordgrass is shorter and more delicate, preferring slightly higher ground. Big Cordgrass grows much taller (up to 10 feet) in freshwater areas, while the dropseed relatives like Sand Dropseed are upland plants that lack the salt tolerance and distinctive marsh habitat of the cordgrasses.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, Saltmarsh Cordgrass is the giant of the group and the only one that thrives in salt water.
Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, prairie cordgrass is by far the tallest and most robust.
Big Cordgrass towers over its Sporobolus relatives - Saltmarsh Cordgrass and Marsh Hay Cordgrass rarely exceed 3 feet tall and have much finer, more delicate appearances.
Unlike its coastal relatives like saltmarsh cordgrass and marsh hay cordgrass which are robust perennials of salt marshes, poverty dropseed is a small annual of dry, sandy inland areas.
Unlike its Sporobolus relatives in New England (the cordgrasses), sand dropseed lives in dry, sandy inland areas rather than salty marshes.
